note:
ISO 2026-W52 runs from December 21 through December 27. To find Jupiter, first identify Leo, trace the Sickle, and locate Regulus in that pattern. Jupiter lies about 2.9° away in ecliptic longitude at the Monday 00:00 UTC snapshot; use the finder to transfer from Regulus to the planet.

**Naked eye:** 🌕 Full Moon · Moon After Yule — 01:28:14 UTC. Bright moonlight favors prominent stars and planets while reducing contrast on faint deep-sky objects. Use Menkar, Algol, Mirfak as the week’s fixed-sky framework.

**Planets:** Moon: Naked eye; magnitude -11.7; direct motion; 86.6% illuminated. Monday 00:00 UTC snapshot. Opposition in ecliptic longitude Dec 24 01:28 UTC. Conjunction with Ceres in ecliptic longitude Dec 25 05:47 UTC. Conjunction with Jupiter in ecliptic longitude Dec 27 16:38 UTC. Conjunction with Uranus in ecliptic longitude Dec 22 02:41 UTC. Mercury: In solar glare; magnitude -0.8; direct motion; 98.5% illuminated. Monday 00:00 UTC snapshot. Venus: Naked eye; magnitude -4.7; direct motion; 42.3% illuminated. Below the horizon at 21:00 local apparent solar time, 45°N. Monday 00:00 UTC snapshot. Mars: Naked eye; magnitude 0.1; direct motion; 91.4% illuminated. Below the horizon at 21:00 local apparent solar time, 45°N. Monday 00:00 UTC snapshot. Ceres: Binoculars; magnitude 7.2; retrograde motion; 99.5% illuminated. Monday 00:00 UTC snapshot. Conjunction with Moon in ecliptic longitude Dec 25 05:47 UTC. Jupiter: Naked eye; magnitude -2.3; retrograde motion; 99.4% illuminated. Below the horizon at 21:00 local apparent solar time, 45°N. Monday 00:00 UTC snapshot. Conjunction with Moon in ecliptic longitude Dec 27 16:38 UTC. Saturn: Naked eye; magnitude 0.7; direct motion; 99.7% illuminated. Monday 00:00 UTC snapshot. Uranus: Binoculars; magnitude 5.6; retrograde motion; 100.0% illuminated. Monday 00:00 UTC snapshot. Conjunction with Moon in ecliptic longitude Dec 22 02:41 UTC. Neptune: Telescope; magnitude 7.7; direct motion; 100.0% illuminated. Monday 00:00 UTC snapshot. Pluto: Substantial telescope; magnitude 14.6; direct motion; 100.0% illuminated. Below the horizon at 21:00 local apparent solar time, 45°N. Monday 00:00 UTC snapshot.

**Binoculars:** Trace Horologium’s charted figure in the finder, then identify β Hor at its charted position. Trace Fornax’s charted figure in the finder, then identify Fornacis at its charted position.

**Small telescope:** Arp 41: consult its dedicated finder and observing story for equipment guidance; PN G138.8+02.8: consult its dedicated finder and observing story for equipment guidance; NGC 1261: consult its dedicated finder and observing story for equipment guidance; Perseus A: consult its dedicated finder and observing story for equipment guidance

**Substantial telescope:** No fixed-sky Calendar object is classified as requiring a substantial telescope this week.

descriptors.name: Full Moon
descriptors.summary: Astronomical lunar phase near opposition to the Sun.
descriptors.body: Full Moon is the lunar phase in which the Moon and Sun are approximately opposite in geocentric ecliptic longitude, so the lunar disk is fully illuminated as seen from Earth.

descriptors.name: Moon After Yule
descriptors.summary: Traditional seasonal designation for the first Full Moon after the December solstice.
descriptors.body: Moon After Yule is the Almanack's traditional seasonal designation for the first Full Moon after the December solstice. It names the seasonal context of the event rather than a separate lunar phase.

story_candidates.dek: β Hor is a star in Hor of catalogue visual magnitude 4.98; its declination determines which latitudes can observe it.
story_candidates.body:
The stored catalogue gives a visual magnitude of 4.98. This is a catalogue value, not a prediction of its brightness this week. Lower magnitudes mean brighter objects; sky brightness and altitude affect whether you can see the star.

Its catalogue position is approximately right ascension 2h 58m and declination -64.1°. These reference coordinates describe its sky location; they are not an observing time or a current altitude.

At the almanac’s default latitude of 45° N, this star does not rise above the geometric horizon. These are geometric calculations from declination, excluding refraction and local obstructions. Darkness and the time of culmination must still be checked for the observing date and your location.

How to find it: Establish the preserved Hor constellation figure from its labeled reference stars, then use the target’s plotted position rather than searching for an isolated star.

Sources: Star Almanack’s stored fixed-object and expanded Bayer catalogues; accepted constellation figures and guiding-star routes. Visibility limits are original geometric calculations from catalogue declination, not weekly predictions.
